Incomer, going-away, driven and overhead

An incomer flies towards you, often from a far trap or a tower, and usually drops as it comes. It can seem to slow down and hang in the air. That tempts you to stop the gun and aim at it like a rifle, a common cause of a miss. It is usually shot while it is still in front of you, before it is overhead. At the moment you fire, the barrels may hide the target (“blot it out”). Many coaches let this happen on such targets: it is usually intended, not a mistake.

A going-away target leaves from near or behind you and flies away. It needs little lead to the side, but it gets small fast and often rises or drops. So you mostly need to shoot a little above it if it rises, or a little below it if it drops, and timing matters: do not wait. In Compak® Sporting a going-away target over side BC is compulsory. It may come from a trap sunk into the ground in front of the stations or from a tower behind them, at least 4 m above the stations.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 3 · Three compulsory trajectories

A driven target is an incomer that passes over your head, like a pheasant pushed by beaters. Many coaches teach it like this. Find it with your eyes early and start moving the gun with it. Bring the gun up from behind the target and through it, fire at the moment the barrels hide it, and keep the gun moving.

An overhead from behind comes over your back and goes away. It is seen late, so many coaches suggest looking back for it before you call. Bring the gun to your shoulder (the mount) as it passes over. Fire as the end of the barrels reaches its front edge, and keep the gun moving after the shot (follow-through).

Tip: “Incoming” and “going away” always describe the target relative to the shooter.

Key points

  • Incomer: comes towards the shooter, usually dropping; take it in front.
  • Going-away: little lead to the side; shoot a little above it if it rises, below if it drops; do not wait.
  • Driven: an incomer over the head; swing through from behind and cover it.
  • Overhead from behind: look back early, mount with it, follow through.
  • A going-away target is compulsory on a Compak® Sporting field.
Stand Talk

  • Coach Take it out in front, before it gets on top of you.

    Meaning: Break the incomer while it is still in front, not when it is overhead.

  • Coach Blot it out and keep swinging.

    Meaning: Let the barrels cover the target at the shot and do not stop the gun.

  • Coach Don't wait on the going-away — it's getting smaller.

    Meaning: Shoot the going-away target promptly, because it is quickly getting further away.

  • Coach It comes from behind you — look back for it early.

    Meaning: It is an overhead from behind; turn the eyes towards it before calling.

For the interpreter
  • Careful: French “en battue” (Italian “in battuta”) means driven game, not the battue target.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. The coach says: “Blot it out.” What should the shooter do?

    1. Wipe the lenses of the safety glasses
    2. Let the barrels cover the target at the shot
    3. Wait until the target disappears from view
    4. Shoot only at the falling pieces
    Answer

    Let the barrels cover the target at the shot

    On incomers, driven and rising targets the gun often covers the clay at the moment of the shot; the coach asks for exactly that.

  2. Why should a going-away target not be left too long?

    1. It quickly gets further away and smaller
    2. The rules allow only three seconds
    3. It always turns into a crosser
    4. The referee calls No Bird after the peak
    Answer

    It quickly gets further away and smaller

    A going-away target gains distance fast, so the longer you wait, the harder it becomes. Three seconds is the release time, not a shooting limit.

  3. What makes a driven target different from an ordinary incomer?

    1. It is always a rabbit
    2. It comes from behind the shooter
    3. It passes over the shooter's head
    4. It is thrown only in Compak® Sporting
    Answer

    It passes over the shooter's head

    Driven means an incomer that comes over the head, like driven game. A target coming from behind is an overhead from behind.
